messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Maya, a 28-year-old teacher, first sought help after months in which ordinary parts of her day had begun to feel contaminated by what happened the spring her ex-partner started stalking her. It had begun outside the elementary school where she taught, when she noticed the same car idling near the curb after dismissal, and then again two days later near her apartment building. He would not approach directly; instead he sent messages, appeared at places she had mentioned, and once she realized that he had been waiting outside her classroom after parent pickup, breathing heavily as if he had just walked fast to keep up with her. That sound still stayed with her. In the weeks that followed, any heavy breathing behind her in a hallway or on a sidewalk could make her body go rigid, because she would immediately feel that same old certainty that she was being watched, tracked, and cornered. Police uniforms had the same effect. When that sense of threat rose in her, the memory did not stay in the background; it came back at once, as if her mind were dragged back to the stalker standing outside her building and the officer taking her report. On the nights when she felt most at risk, the memory was hardest to keep at bay and would surface in vivid fragments she could not push away. When officers took her report, the authority presence was meant to reassure her, but instead it became tied to the worst moments of her ordeal; now even the sight of police outside a store or near her school could make her stomach drop, because it brought back the helplessness of needing protection and not feeling safe.  

What frightened Maya most was how quickly those cues could open the memory. Some parts of the stalking were vivid to her in a way that felt almost unbearable: the specific evening he stood across from her building in the dark, the glare of headlights, the sense that she could not predict where he would appear next. Other parts were blank, as if her mind had erased them, and she hated that she could not put the whole thing into words for her partner or the police report she had tried to revisit. She knew what had happened, but when she tried to tell it, the account broke into fragments — a text message, a car door closing, his breathing, a police car arriving — which would appear suddenly without warning and then vanish before she could hold onto them. Those fragments themselves were distressing; they left her feeling flooded and on edge, and once she was overwhelmed in that way, she became even more likely to notice signs of the stalking everywhere. An unusually quiet corridor at school, a silence on the street after the bell rang, or the sense that someone was following her between parked cars could make her mind jump back to those snippets, and the memory would arrive in pieces that sharpened her sense that danger was near.  

As the weeks turned into months, Maya began to interpret the whole experience through the belief that people could not be trusted. She had once been warm and easy with parents, colleagues, and neighbors, but now she felt her life had been destroyed by the trauma, and that conviction hardened each time she found herself checking over her shoulder before unlocking her car or scanning the grocery aisle for unfamiliar men. Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that she could not trust her own judgment, almost anything could feel like a warning sign: a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her in the school corridor. Those appraisals made ordinary situations feel mined for danger, and even small ambiguities began to operate as triggers that set her vigilance surging. She came to believe she had to be on guard all the time, because letting her attention drift even for a minute felt like inviting him — or someone like him — back into her life. That mistrust did not remain abstract; it altered the world around her. Strangers approaching her in ordinary situations felt threatening, not because they were doing anything overtly harmful, but because her mind had learned to treat any approach as a possible prelude to being watched, followed, or trapped. At the same time, the things that reminded her of the stalking did not stay limited to the obvious. Heavy breathing in a classroom doorway, the sudden quiet of an empty parking lot after dismissal, even a police cruiser parked near the school could pull her back into those memories, and the memory itself would amplify the sense of danger until she felt certain she needed to move, leave, or look for exits.  

By the time she arrived in therapy, Maya was still functioning at work, but in a narrowed, exhausted way. She had started arriving early to check the building, avoiding the parking lot until other staff were around, and arranging for her partner to walk her to her car after late meetings. She had not told many people why, because speaking about it felt impossible and because her mistrust made her wary of being misunderstood. She described feeling trapped between the knowledge that the stalking had ended and the feeling that it could restart at any moment. What finally brought her in was a day at school when she heard heavy breathing just behind her in an empty hallway, turned, and for a split second saw no one — only the silence and the blank space where he might have been. The fear that surged through her was so strong that it brought back a burst of images she could not later fully describe, and afterward she spent the rest of the day scanning every sound, every face, every shadow. She came to treatment hoping to learn how to feel safe again, but what she feared most was that her guard would have to stay up forever, and that if she ever let it down, the life she had before would be gone for good.
